The final is regenerated from your recording: a new performance of the scene, not a copy of the footage.

posts.text:
Joe Rogan figured it might just be a conspiracy theory that AI companies were secretly buying millions of books, scanning them, and destroying the originals.

Then Jamie looked it up. It’s 100% real.

ROGAN: “Oh my god, it’s true.”

The deeper they dug, the more upset Rogan got.

Anthropic had an internal code name for the operation: “Project Panama.”

THE INTERNAL MEMO SAID:

“Project Panama is our effort to destructively scan all the books in the world.”

“We don’t want it to be known that we are working on this.”

ROGAN’S REACTION:

“Meaning they know that they’re doing something that will cause people to f***ing freak out and revolt.”

“The training data is other people’s work. It’s books. That’s what’s insane.”

“The idea that you could… burn all the books so that your company succeeds and other ones don’t is the problem we’re talking about.”

WHAT HAPPENED:

Anthropic needed a mountain of books to train its AI. So it bought millions of them. Workers cut the spines off, scanned every page, and threw the books out when they were done.

They wanted to keep this a secret, but then a group of authors sued in a case known as Bartz v. Anthropic. To Rogan’s dismay, the judge ruled the scanning was “fair use,” so Anthropic was allowed to do it.

Where the company got in trouble was the pirated stuff. On top of the books it bought, Anthropic had downloaded millions more from pirate sites for free, and the judge wouldn’t let that go.

That ended up costing them $1.5 billion, the biggest copyright settlement in U.S. history, or about $3,000 per pirated book.

Barry Sanders retired with one fax, 1,457 yards short of the all-time rushing record.

Two years earlier, the Detroit Lions had made him the highest-paid player in the NFL. About $35 million over six years, with an $11 million signing bonus.

Then the Lions came after $7.37 million of that bonus.

In the video below, Sanders explains why he walked away. And why the record didn't matter.

July 1999. He was 31. The year before, he ran for over 2,000 yards.

No press conference. A statement to his hometown paper in Wichita, a call to the team the day before training camp, and a flight to London.

Detroit was furious.

Miami reportedly wanted to trade for him. The Lions' answer, as former teammate Lomas Brown tells it: either you play for us, or you don't play for anybody.

So he didn't.

The Lions filed a grievance for $7.37 million. An arbitrator gave them $5.5 million - paid in pieces, and only for as long as he stayed retired.

He stayed retired.

Keep this part.

A contract you can't walk out of isn't security. It's a cage with a salary.

The Lions owned six years of his career on paper. They couldn't own his will to play them.

Sanders gave back millions to leave on his own terms. Three years later, Emmitt Smith broke the record.

Sanders never played another snap.

Would you give back $5.5 million to walk away on your terms - or play out the contract?
